beats.text: On the twenty-eighth of May, 1998, a mountain in [Chagai](/ʧˈɑɡi/) turned white. Pakistan had tested its first nuclear bombs.
Almost nobody was talking about what was already in that ground. Fifteen million tonnes of copper. Twenty-six million ounces of gold.
In 1993, a caretaker government gave a foreign miner seventy-five percent.
In 2011, [Balochistan](/bəlˈOʧɪstˌɑn/) refused the mining lease. In 2013, the Supreme Court voided the whole deal.
Then a treaty with Australia sent Pakistan to a World Bank tribunal. And in 2019, the bill came in. Nearly six billion dollars.
In 2022, Pakistan traded the penalty for a new partnership, and wrote a law to protect it.
The world needs copper, and the lenders lined up.
Then, in 2026, the operator slowed down. And reports say the date could slip to 2030.
Thirty years on, the copper produced is zero.
